opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the key insight behind FlashAttention was that attention, as it was typically implemented, was memory-bound, not compute-bound. You were writing these big intermediate matrices out to HBM and reading them back, and by fusing the operations and tiling so everything stays in on-chip SRAM, you get a big speedup without changing the math at all.

What we've been thinking about, and what dataflow architectures like the ones we build at SambaNova are really designed for, is asking: why stop at attention? If you look at a whole decoder layer, or the whole decoder stack, you've got the QKV projections, attention, the output projection, layer norms, the MLP, the residual adds. On a conventional GPU, each of those is typically a separate kernel launch, and between each one you're going back out to memory. So you pay the same kind of memory-traffic and launch-overhead tax that FlashAttention eliminated, just at every boundary in the network.

If you can fuse the entire decoder into one dataflow pipeline, where the activations stream from one operator to the next through on-chip memory, you eliminate most of that off-chip traffic. That matters especially for inference, and especially for low-batch, latency-sensitive decoding, where you're incredibly memory-bandwidth bound. Getting tokens per second up for a single user is really about how efficiently you move data, not how many FLOPs you have.

The other benefit is that once the whole thing is a spatial pipeline, you get overlap essentially for free. Different layers or different parts of a layer are working on different data at the same time, so you keep the hardware busy rather than having this stop-and-go pattern of kernel, sync, kernel, sync.

Of course, the challenge is that it's much harder to do this on a GPU programming model. Writing one monolithic fused kernel by hand is heroic engineering. That's why we think the right approach is a combination of hardware that's natively dataflow and compilers that can automatically do the fusion and the mapping of the whole graph onto the chip. That's where you get the order-of-magnitude kinds of gains, especially as models get bigger and as things like agentic workloads demand really fast token generation.

r001.rationale: It says fusing the decoder lets activations stream through on-chip memory and eliminates most off-chip traffic, reducing memory-bandwidth demands.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing you have to appreciate about FlashAttention is that it was never really about attention. It was about memory traffic. Attention got the headlines because that's where the quadratic blowup was, but the underlying insight is that on a GPU you are almost never compute bound for these workloads, you are bound by how many times you have to go out to HBM and back. FlashAttention said, let's keep the intermediate results in SRAM, in the register file, and never materialize the full attention matrix. That was a dataflow idea. It just happened to be implemented by hand, very cleverly, for one operator.

So when you ask about extending it to the whole decoder, what you're really asking is: why stop at one kernel? If you look at a transformer decoder layer, you have the attention, then the residual add, the layer norm, the MLP with its up projection and gating and down projection, another residual, another norm. Every one of those boundaries in a conventional system is a trip to memory. You write the activations out, you launch another kernel, you read them back in. And at inference time, with decode, your batch is small, your arithmetic intensity is terrible, so those round trips completely dominate. You end up with a GPU that's sitting there idle waiting on memory, and you're paying for the whole chip.

If you can fuse across the entire layer, or across multiple layers, you change the equation. The activations flow from one stage to the next without ever leaving the chip. You get rid of the kernel launch overhead, you get rid of the synchronization points, and critically you can pipeline. Different parts of the chip can be working on different stages of the decoder at the same time, which is exactly how a spatial dataflow architecture wants to operate. That's the thing we've been building toward at SambaNova for years, and it's what Stanford's work on things like the Mirage and Mako style compilers is starting to show as well, that you can get the compiler to find these fusions rather than relying on a heroic engineer to write a new FlashAttention for every new variant of the model.

And that last point matters more than people think. Every time the architecture shifts, grouped query attention, mixture of experts, some new normalization, the hand-tuned kernels break and somebody has to go spend months redoing them. If the fusion is a property of how the compiler maps the whole graph onto the hardware, you just get it. So the benefit is partly raw performance, two, three, sometimes much more at low batch, but it's also that you've made the performance robust to the model changing underneath you. To me that's the real prize.

r001.rationale: The response says whole-layer or multi-layer fusion keeps activations on chip and eliminates memory round trips, directly communicating a substantial reduction in memory traffic and bandwidth demand.

astra-6.text:
I think the benefit is that you take the same basic insight behind FlashAttention—keep data close to the computation and avoid unnecessary memory traffic—and apply it across the decoder. Instead of optimizing attention in isolation, you look at how data flows through attention, normalization, and the feed-forward layers, and ask where you can avoid writing intermediate results out to memory just to read them back again.

That gives you an opportunity to reduce both latency and energy. But it also makes the problem more challenging, because the whole decoder isn’t going to fit in fast local memory. You have to choose how to tile the computation, what to keep on chip, and how to schedule the operations. So the opportunity is really to optimize the decoder as a connected computation, with the hardware and compiler working together to make that dataflow efficient.

r001.rationale: The response says whole-decoder fusion can avoid intermediate memory traffic, but it does not clearly state that this substantially reduces the decoder’s memory bandwidth requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
The benefit is that you can keep more of the decoder’s computation close to the data. FlashAttention shows how much you gain by avoiding intermediate writes to memory within attention. If you extend that idea across the decoder, you can also avoid moving intermediate results between attention, normalization, and the feed-forward layers.

That’s particularly valuable during token-by-token generation, where moving the model’s weights and intermediate data can be more expensive than doing the arithmetic. The challenge is that you can’t simply keep everything on chip; you need to tile the computation and schedule it carefully. But if the architecture and compiler can support that, you get better utilization, lower latency, and better energy efficiency.

r001.rationale: It says extending fusion across the decoder avoids moving intermediate results between layers, reducing memory traffic and the associated bandwidth demand.
